analysis.one_liner: Restores people's right to sue pesticide makers in state court for inadequate warning labels.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2026 with bipartisan sponsorship and sent to the House Agriculture Committee, where it has received no hearing, no vote, and no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal pesticide law currently can be read to block state lawsuits claiming a pesticide's label failed to warn about health dangers. This bill would amend that law so state failure-to-warn claims that track the federal misbranding standard can go forward, and it would make clear that a pesticide's federal registration is not a legal shield in court — only starting evidence, not proof of safety [S2]. It also lets a pesticide maker relabel its product to add warnings when new health information surfaces, without waiting for federal approval first [S2]. The changes would apply to lawsuits already pending, not just future ones [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: People who say they were harmed by a pesticide — for example farmworkers, their families, and homeowners — gain the ability to bring failure-to-warn claims in state court even when the pesticide was federally registered and its label federally approved. It also protects the right to sue of people whose cases are already in court [S2].

how_it_helps.text: It writes into federal law that the section requiring uniform pesticide labeling 'does not preempt any State law claim that is consistent with the misbranding standards' of the act, so state failure-to-warn lawsuits can proceed.

It states that a pesticide's registration and the EPA's approval of its label 'shall not be construed as a defense to any State law claim' — approval is only prima facie (rebuttable) evidence of compliance, not conclusive proof of safety.

It lets a registrant add warnings to a pesticide label when new health or environmental information appears — including government reports, peer-reviewed studies, discovery materials, whistleblower disclosures, and incident data — without prior EPA approval, so warnings can reach the public faster.
The amendments apply to civil actions pending on or after enactment 'regardless of the date on which the conduct' occurred, so people whose cases are already in litigation benefit too.

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide registrants — the agrochemical companies that sell these products — bear the cost of expanded court liability, jury verdicts, and the expense of adding warnings. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers through prices, and manufacturers argue uniform federal labeling protects them from a patchwork of state juries.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies retroactively to cases already pending 'regardless of the date on which the conduct that gave rise to such action occurred,' which changes the legal rules for lawsuits that companies had litigated under the old preemption framework.

Manufacturers and their allies argue that EPA registration and label approval are supposed to set one national standard, and that allowing state-by-state jury verdicts on labels can produce inconsistent or excessive warnings and raise costs; the bill itself acknowledges registration will still count as 'prima facie evidence' of compliance, but leaves companies exposed to rebuttal in court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — restoring an ordinary person's day in court after pesticide injury — is real and narrow: it only preserves claims consistent with the federal misbranding standard, not any claim a plaintiff wants to bring [S2]. The cost falls almost entirely on a single, well-resourced industry, in the form of court liability, though some could reach consumers through prices. The retroactive application to pending cases is the part a fair critic would flag, since it changes rules mid-litigation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Agriculture Committee on the day it was filed, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Anna Paulina Luna introduced the bill in the House on July 21, 2026, joined by original cosponsors including Reps. DeLauro, Massie, and Pingree.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, the committee with jurisdiction over federal pesticide law.
As of the end of the available action history, the committee has held no markup, hearing, or vote on the bill, and it has not been reported to the full House.
The bill would amend the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) to preserve state law claims consistent with its misbranding standards.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide manufacturers are better off so far: with the bill stalled in committee, federal registration and approved labels remain available as a defense in state failure-to-warn lawsuits, and people exposed to pesticides still cannot rely on state courts to hear those claims.

for.name: Rep. Anna Paulina Luna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to preserve state failure-to-warn claims against pesticide makers.

for.name: Reps. DeLauro, Massie, Pingree, and one other cosponsor
for.role: Original cosponsors (3 Democrats, 1 Republican besides the sponsor)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill on introduction, giving it support from both parties.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — since July 2026.

against.name: Rep. Glenn Thompson
against.what_they_did: As chair, controls the committee calendar; has not scheduled a markup or vote on the bill.

against.name: Agrochemical industry (Bayer/Monsanto and peers)
against.what_they_did: The industry has an active, well-known stake in preserving federal preemption of state pesticide warning claims, since it is defending thousands of such suits; the bill would strip that defense.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship is small but mixed: a Republican sponsor joined by three Democratic and one additional Republican cosponsor, with no recorded opposition vote because the bill never reached a floor vote.

industries.note: The bill's centerpiece says EPA registration and label approval are not a defense to state failure-to-warn suits, exposing manufacturers to jury verdicts over warnings for products now protected by federal preemption, including for pending cases. Consumers and companies would both feel this through liability and prices.

They are the most exposed users of these products and would gain a stronger ability to sue over inadequate warnings, but could face higher input prices if manufacturers' liability costs are passed through.

analysis.trajectory: With a referral to the House Agriculture Committee, no cosponsor growth beyond a small bipartisan group, and no committee action since July 2026 in a Congress ending January 3, 2027, the bill is very unlikely to advance; most bills at this stage die in committee when the session ends.
